summary: This defines a RobotPet class whose battery level is guarded by a property setter, then three subclasses \u2014 RobotCat, RobotBird, and RobotDog \u2014 that each override show_talent with their own species trick. Nothing is printed yet; the file just supplies the classes that the chapter's unit tests will exercise.

lines.text: Even inside __init__ this assignment goes through the battery setter rather than storing the number directly, so a pet created with a battery of 250 is clamped the moment it is born.
The setter is the single place where the rule "battery stays between 0 and 100" lives, which is exactly the kind of behaviour a unit test can pin down with a couple of out-of-range values.
charge does no checking of its own; it reads the current level, adds to it, and hands the result back to the setter, which caps it at 100.

lines.code: return f"{self.name} performs a generic trick!"
lines.text: The base class returns its message instead of printing it, which is what lets a test compare the result against an expected string.
Each subclass inherits the name, battery, and charge behaviour untouched and redefines only show_talent \u2014 the whole point of subclassing here is that one method differs per species.
